question: What's the best GovWin alternative for a small government contractor?

claude.answer:
I'll research current options for you.## Short answer

For most small government contractors, **HigherGov is the best starting point** — it has a genuinely usable free tier and low-cost paid plans, and it replaces the core function people buy GovWin for (finding opportunities, tracking awards, researching competitors and teaming partners). If you need more, **GovTribe** is the next step up, and **EZGovOpps** is the budget option if you specifically care about IDIQ/task-order visibility.

The real issue is that GovWin isn't priced for you. Buyer transaction data compiled by Civic IQ (citing Vendr) puts GovWin IQ at roughly **$13,000–$119,000/year, averaging ~$29,000**, and it's built around analyst-curated pre-RFP intelligence for large primes with dedicated capture teams. Independent comparisons note that tools like GovTribe or HigherGov can cover the core federal feed for under ~10% of that cost.

## Pick based on your market

| Your situation | Best fit |
|---|---|
| Federal, 1–5 people, tight budget | HigherGov (free tier first), then GovTribe |
| Federal, chasing task orders on IDIQs/GWACs | EZGovOpps or Govly |
| State/local/education (SLED) | BidPrime or Pursuit.us — GovWin's SLED analyst data is its real differentiator, so SLED-focused alternatives matter more here |
| You want to know what agencies actually buy | GovSpend (purchase-order-level spend data) |
| Mid-size federal with a capture process | Federal Compass |

Reported pricing for the small-business tier tools generally lands in the **$99–$399/month** range (GovTribe and BidPrime are commonly listed around $99–$299/mo), but confirm directly with vendors — published numbers move and most of them don't post real pricing.

## Two things worth knowing before you shop

**1. Almost every "best GovWin alternative" article is written by a vendor.** SamSearch, Civic IQ, Pursuit, Procura Federal, and GovContractFinder all publish comparison posts that rank themselves #1. Treat those as marketing, not research. G2 reviews and free trials are more useful signals.

**2. You may not need a paid tool at all yet.** SAM.gov is free and lists 50,000+ active opportunities with filtering by NAICS, set-aside, and agency, and GSA eBuy is free if you hold a Schedule. If you're pre-revenue in federal or bidding fewer than a handful of deals a year, a paid subscription mostly buys you *time saved*, not access. The honest test: if a tool doesn't save you enough hours or surface enough pre-RFP lead time to pay for itself in one win, it's premature.

## My recommendation

Start free on HigherGov plus SAM.gov alerts for 30–60 days. If your bottleneck turns out to be *finding* opportunities, upgrade within HigherGov or trial GovTribe. If your bottleneck is *knowing about them 6–12 months early* — which is what GovWin genuinely does better than anyone — no cheap tool fully replaces that, and you'd be better off investing in agency relationships and teaming with primes than in software.

One caveat: I couldn't verify current pricing for HigherGov, GovTribe, or EZGovOpps directly before hitting a search limit, so treat the dollar figures above as ballpark and confirm on vendor sites.

question: What's a cheaper alternative to GovTribe?

I'll look into GovTribe and its competitors for you.# Cheaper Alternatives to GovTribe

**Short answer: HigherGov** is the alternative most people land on — it's comparably priced or cheaper at the entry level and has a free tier.

## First, what GovTribe actually costs

GovTribe's published self-service plans are billed annually: Launch at $1,500/year (federal only, 1 user, 50-record exports), Launch Plus at $1,900/year (adds state and local), Growth at $5,000/year (federal only, 5 users, 3,000-record exports), and Growth Plus at $6,000/year, with Scale as a custom tier.

## The main contenders

**HigherGov — the strongest value pick**

HigherGov's own comparison page lists pricing of $500 for Individual and $2,500 for Team, versus Govtribe's $500 Individual and $3,000 Team. Third-party listings corroborate the tiers: Starter at $500 for a single user, Standard at $2,500 for up to 10 users, and Leader at $5,000 for up to 50 users, with a free trial available.

The data coverage argument is arguably stronger than the price argument: HigherGov tracks opportunities from more than 200 sources, while GovTribe and most similar platforms only source from sam.gov and grants.gov — including SBIR opportunities, contract forecasts from hundreds of agencies, more than 7,000 state/local/education agencies, and federal sources like DLA DIBBS. One review roundup notes it "offers a genuinely useful free tier" — so you can test it at zero cost before committing.

**Worth knowing about the market**

An independent comparison frames GovTribe as a well-priced federal opportunity tracker that is federal-first, sourced mainly from SAM.gov and grants.gov, and thin on state and local. So "cheaper" depends on what you're actually missing.

**Not cheaper:** EZGovOpps starts at $2,695 per year despite marketing itself on affordability, and GovWin IQ sits well above GovTribe.

## Free options

If your budget is genuinely zero, the underlying government sources are free: **SAM.gov** (active solicitations and entity registration), **USAspending.gov** and **FPDS-NG** (award and spending history), and **grants.gov**. GovTribe and HigherGov are largely aggregation, alerting, and analysis layers on top of this public data — you lose the saved searches, alerts, competitor dashboards, and pipeline tools, but the raw data costs nothing. Both SAM.gov and USAspending also offer public APIs if you have any technical capacity in-house.

## My recommendation

Start with **HigherGov's free tier** alongside SAM.gov alerts. If the free tier covers you, you've saved $1,500/year. If you need more, the $500 Starter is a third of GovTribe's Launch plan, and the multi-user Standard tier at $2,500 undercuts GovTribe's Growth at $5,000 while covering more users and more data sources.

One caveat before you switch: a review roundup notes that with HigherGov, breadth can mean more to filter, and analysis and contact intelligence are lighter than dedicated capture or SLED-sales platforms, with no built-in proposal writing. If you're pure-play federal and happy with GovTribe's interface, the savings at the single-user level may be modest enough that switching costs aren't worth it.

question: How do I decide whether to bid on a SAM.gov opportunity?

claude.answer:
I'll check current SAM.gov specifics so the framework reflects how the system actually works today.Built you a working decision kit, and here's the framework behind it.

[Download the SAM.gov Bid/No-Bid Decision Kit (Excel)](computer:///mnt/user-data/outputs/SAMgov_Bid_No-Bid_Decision_Kit.xlsx)

## The three-stage filter

**Stage 1 — Hard gates (binary, 5 minutes).** These are pass/fail; a single "No" kills the pursuit no matter how attractive it looks. The big ones: active SAM registration, set-aside eligibility, NAICS/size-standard match, required vehicle or clearances, bonding, and whether you missed a mandatory step like a site visit or Q&A cutoff.

Two gates people get wrong:

- **Registration timing.** An offeror is required to be registered in SAM when submitting an offer or quotation and at time of award, and processing time should be taken into consideration when registering. A 2025 FAR Council rule clarified this — companies need to be registered at "two points" only, at time of offer submission and at time of award, ending years of confusion created by a 2018 amendment to FAR 52.204-7. Don't find a great RFP with a lapsed registration and 10 days to respond.
- **Prime vs. sub.** A useful rule of thumb is to prime only when you can perform at least 60% of the work, demonstrate 3–5 strong past-performance examples aligned to major tasks, meet all technical, staffing, and management requirements, and deliver without excessive reliance on teaming partners. If you can't meet those conditions, pursue it as a subcontractor or drop it from your pipeline. "No bid" and "no interest" aren't the same thing.

**Stage 2 — Weighted score.** Twelve criteria across customer knowledge, capability fit, past performance, competitive position, price/margin, capacity, and strategic value. Score each 1–5; the sheet weights and totals it, then recommends Bid / Bid-if-conditions-met / No bid. Thresholds are 75% and 60%, editable. The industry norm is similar — one common checklist uses 30 questions scored 0–2 for a max of 60, with 36 (60%) as the minimum recommended score to bid.

The highest-signal input isn't on most checklists: **did you talk to the customer before the solicitation dropped?** If your first contact with the program is reading the RFP on SAM.gov, your realistic win probability is in the single digits. Incumbents and shapers have been talking to that contracting officer for a year.

Also score yourself against *their* scorecard, not your own. Find the evaluation criteria section — every serious solicitation has one — and note the weighting, which will read something like technical approach 40 points, past performance 30, price 20, small-business participation 10. If 30 points ride on past performance and yours is thin, no amount of writing quality fixes that.

**Stage 3 — Pursuit economics.** Proposals cost real money. The third tab computes expected value (contract value × margin × honest P-win) against proposal cost (hours × loaded rate + B&P), plus the breakeven win probability you'd need to justify the effort. A 20% P-win on a $500K contract at 15% margin is $15K of expected value — if the proposal costs $13K to write, that's a bad trade even though it "passed" the scorecard.

## Red flags that should make you walk

- Short response window on a large, complex requirement — usually a wired recompete
- Spec language lifted from one vendor's product literature or brand-name justifications
- LPTA award on a service you can't commoditize
- 40+ awardees expected on an IDIQ with no guaranteed minimum beyond the $2,500 floor
- Requirement drifts from your core — chasing every opportunity you see instead of focusing on core capability, and overestimating your team's ability to perform to government standards, is the classic small-business mistake

## One habit that compounds

Tab 4 is a pipeline log — record every opportunity you gate, including the no-bids and the reason. After 30 entries you'll see your actual win rate by agency, set-aside type, and contract size, and you can replace the generic weights in the scorecard with ones calibrated to your own history. That's the point where bid/no-bid stops being gut feel.

Want me to tune the weights for your specific NAICS, company size, or target agencies?

HigherGov, GovTribe, SamSearch and similar offer AI solicitation analysis, but HigherGov starts around $500/year and GovTribe around $1,500/year. Most have trials rather than a genuine free tier.

**My suggestion:** start with the free APEX Accelerator for your first few bids, and use me for fast turnaround on compliance matrices and deadline extraction. Want to paste a notice now?

question: How do I know if a Sources Sought notice is worth responding to?

claude.answer:
## First, understand what you're buying with your time

A Sources Sought (or RFI) response is a marketing and market-shaping document, not a bid. The agency uses responses to decide two things: whether to set the work aside for small business (the "Rule of Two" — if two or more capable small businesses respond at fair market prices, FAR 19.502-2 generally requires a set-aside), and what the requirements/scope should look like. That means the real return isn't "winning" the sources sought — it's influencing the set-aside decision, shaping the SOW toward your strengths, and getting on the contracting officer's radar before the competition starts.

A decent response costs 4–12 hours. Judge whether it's worth it against that number.

## Green flags — respond

- **You can honestly claim past performance that matches the core scope**, ideally same agency or same work type, within the last 3 years.
- **Your socioeconomic status could trigger or sustain a set-aside** (8(a), SDVOSB, WOSB, HUBZone). Here your response has leverage even if you're not the strongest technically — you're a data point in the Rule of Two count.
- **The notice is detailed** — draft SOW/PWS attached, specific NAICS, questions about labor categories, estimated value, period of performance. Detail signals the agency is genuinely planning and hasn't locked the approach yet.
- **It asks substantive questions** ("What contract type do you recommend?", "Are the proposed quantities feasible?"). Agencies that want input are agencies you can influence.
- **The incumbent contract is ending and you've been tracking it** — you know the ceiling, the incumbent, and the pain points.
- **Timing fits** — RFP likely 3–9 months out, which gives you room to build teaming and capture.

## Red flags — probably skip or send a thin response

- **Extremely short, vague notice with a 3–5 day turnaround.** Often a compliance checkbox before a sole-source justification or a decision already made.
- **Brand-name-or-equal language with one brand's specs reproduced verbatim**, or requirements that only one firm's product configuration satisfies.
- **It's a re-posted sources sought for a contract the incumbent has held for 15 years**, and the requirements mirror the incumbent's exact capability statement.
- **The NAICS/size standard excludes you**, or the work is outside your actual delivery capability and you'd be assembling a team from scratch.
- **No point of contact other than a generic inbox**, no questions asked, no page limits — signals low engagement.
- **You have zero relevant past performance.** Responding anyway isn't harmful, but it's low-yield; your time is better spent subcontracting to someone who does.

## The decision test

Ask three questions:

1. **If this becomes an RFP tomorrow, would I bid?** If no, don't respond. If yes, respond — you need the shaping opportunity.
2. **Can I change the outcome?** Either by moving the set-aside decision, or by getting a requirement added/removed that favors me. If the answer is "no influence possible," the value drops to pure relationship-building.
3. **Is this on my target account list?** Responses to agencies you're actively pursuing have compounding value — the CO starts recognizing your name. Scattershot responses across unrelated agencies mostly don't.

## A middle path worth using

For marginal opportunities, send a **short-form response**: two pages, capability statement plus three relevant past performance references plus explicit answers to any questions asked. You get counted for Rule of Two purposes and you're in the file, for about 90 minutes of work. Reserve the full-effort response — recommendations on contract type, risk commentary, suggested requirement changes — for opportunities you genuinely intend to pursue.

One tactical note: always answer the questions the notice actually asks, in the order asked, and always state your socioeconomic certifications, UEI, CAGE code, and whether you'd bid as prime or sub. COs frequently discard responses that are just a generic marketing brochure.

question: What software helps small businesses with bid/no-bid decisions in government contracting?

claude.answer:
I'll research this for you.## What these tools actually do

Bid/no-bid software sits between opportunity discovery and proposal writing. The core function is to assess RFP fit and probability of win (pWin) against your capabilities before you commit proposal resources, with better tools extracting Sections C, L, and M automatically and generating compliance matrices. Capture management software more broadly helps contractors identify opportunities early, qualify them, research incumbents and competitors, coordinate teaming, and track bid/no-bid decisions.

## Budget tier (realistic for most small businesses)

| Tool | Approximate cost | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **SAM.gov** | Free | The official, free portal for federal procurement opportunities valued over $25,000, providing visibility into active solicitations, award data, and past performance |
| **Set-Aside Pro** | $299/year | Helps small enterprises discover and monitor federal opportunities |
| **SellToState** | $49/month or $490/year, no per-user fees | Offers an API/MCP endpoint for querying tender information through AI assistants |
| **GovTribe** | ~$1,500–$6,000/year | Federal pipeline tracking, vendor/agency profiles, award analytics, saved searches and alerts |

## Mid-tier with actual bid/no-bid scoring

- **CLEATUS** — analyzes past awards, compliance complexity, and competitive data to assess contract viability, producing a compliance score and similar-contract comparisons. Its CRM tracks opportunities from capture to award with Kanban boards, amendment/deadline alerts, and collaboration features.
- **Capture2Proposal** — combines business intelligence and capture management in one customizable solution spanning intelligence, capture, proposal, and teaming.
- **Procura Federal** — from $399/month on an annual plan, aimed at small business prime contractors and BD teams of 1–5, going beyond tracking to analyze opportunity fit in long attachment packages.
- **CaptureStar / CaptureExec (BIT Solutions)** — CaptureStar is positioned for startup and small-sized government contractors, with the broader platform aimed at teams moving from "2 salespeople and a spreadsheet" to a scalable system.
- **Procurement Sciences (PSci.AI)** — markets AI-powered decisioning tools to focus resources on the most promising opportunities.

## Enterprise (usually overkill for small firms)

GovWin IQ pricing starts around $10,000/year and scales significantly for enterprise teams, and GovSpend is custom-quoted, typically $3,000–$6,000 per user annually for teams of 5 to 10. Unanet and Bloomberg Government fall in similar territory.

## Practical guidance

**Prioritize these features at small scale:** free tiers, set-aside filtering, email alerts, and affordable pricing. If you handle CUI, note that FedRAMP Moderate or equivalent security controls and CMMC-aligned practices are often required.

**Keep expectations calibrated.** Deltek's 2021 Clarity GovCon Industry Study found a median competitive-proposal win rate of just 35%, with small businesses at 33%. Software improves *which* bids you chase; it doesn't fix weak past performance or absent agency relationships. Firms with active capture programs may have already influenced Section L by the time your team first reads it — so the real leverage is pre-RFP positioning, not faster triage.

**Three caveats on the sources above:** much of the comparison content online is published by the vendors themselves (GovEagle, SamSearch, Procura Federal, GovContractFinder all rank their own products), so treat rankings skeptically and demand trials. Second, AI should be treated as a tool that enhances human decision-making rather than replacing it. Third, before buying anything, a free, well-built bid/no-bid scorecard (incumbent known? past performance match? set-aside eligible? customer relationship? realistic pWin above ~30%?) plus SAM.gov and your local APEX Accelerator will outperform expensive software used passively.

question: How can I find SAM.gov opportunities that don't have a NAICS code?

claude.answer:
I'll look into this for you.## Short answer

SAM.gov's UI has no "NAICS is blank" filter — the NAICS filter only lets you include codes, never exclude or require-empty. So you have to pull the data and filter it yourself. There are three practical routes, best to worst.

### Why these notices exist

NAICS isn't mandatory on every notice type. The Get Opportunities API's `ptype` values include Justification (u), Pre-solicitation (p), Award Notice (a), Sources Sought (r), Special Notice (s), Solicitation (o), Sale of Surplus Property (g), Combined Synopsis/Solicitation (k), and Intent to Bundle Requirements (i) — and the no-NAICS records cluster heavily in Special Notices, Justifications (J&A), Sale of Surplus Property, and Award Notices. These are exactly the notices that keyword/NAICS-driven competitors never see, which is usually why people go looking for them.

---

### Option 1 — Get Opportunities Public API (most reliable)

The `ncode` (NAICS) parameter is optional, so you just omit it and filter `naicsCode == null` on your side. Key constraints: `api_key` and `postedFrom`/`postedTo` (MM/dd/yyyy) are required, the posted-date range cannot exceed 1 year, and `limit` maxes out at 1000 records per page with a default of 1. You request a public API key from the Account Details page on SAM.gov.

I wrote and syntax-tested a script for you — [find_no_naics.py](computer:///tmp/find_no_naics.py):

```bash
export SAM_API_KEY=your_key
python find_no_naics.py 10/01/2025 10/31/2025 no_naics.csv
```

It pages through everything in the window, keeps only records where `naicsCode` is null/empty (it also checks the `naics[]` array fallback), and writes a CSV with the notice ID, title, type, agency, deadline, and the direct SAM.gov link. Go month-by-month rather than a full year — you'll stay under the daily request cap.

To target only the likely buckets, add `"ptype": "s"` (Special Notice) or `"u"` (Justification) to the `extra` dict in `fetch_page`.

### Option 2 — Daily full CSV extract (no API key, no rate limit)

SAM.gov publishes the entire Contract Opportunities list as a public daily CSV extract requiring no key and no rate limit; the `ContractOpportunitiesFullCSV.csv` file is discoverable through SAM.gov's public file-extract listing on Data Services. Download it and filter the empty NAICS column:

```bash
# find the NAICS column index, then keep rows where it's empty
awk -F'","' 'NR==1{for(i=1;i<=NF;i++) if($i ~ /NaicsCode/) c=i; print; next} $c==""' \
    ContractOpportunitiesFullCSV.csv > no_naics.csv
```

One caveat: this file has broken before — one tooling vendor reported the upstream generator failed and regenerated the file as a header-only stub for several weeks. Check the byte count/row count before trusting a run.

### Option 3 — UI workaround

Run a Contract Opportunities search with **no** NAICS filter (narrow by date, notice type, or agency instead), then use the **Download** button to export results and sort/filter the blank NAICS column in Excel. Fine for a one-off; it caps out on result count and can't be scheduled.

---

**Practical tip:** set up a saved search on Special Notices + your agencies with no NAICS filter at all, and run the API script weekly against the prior 7 days. The no-NAICS set is small enough per week that you can eyeball every title.

question: What's the best way to track federal contract recompetes?

claude.answer:
I'll research current approaches and tools for this.## The core idea

Recompetes are the only truly predictable opportunities in federal contracting, because the expiration date of the current contract is public. Award records in USAspending and FPDS include the contract end date and any option periods, so you can identify expiring contracts long before a new solicitation is posted on SAM.gov. Everything below is about systematically harvesting those dates and turning them into a pipeline 18–24 months ahead of RFP release.

## Free sources (start here)

**SAM.gov contract data.** Note that the workflow changed recently: GSA decommissioned the ezSearch function within FPDS.gov on February 24, 2026, with all ezSearch functionality moving to SAM.gov. The migration started as a soft launch in July 2025, and remaining government data feeds are scheduled to sunset later in FY2026. If you have bookmarked FPDS searches or scripts hitting the old endpoints, they need rebuilding. The fields that matter in an award record are period of performance, incumbent UEI, face value vs. obligated-to-date, set-aside type, and number of offers received.

**USAspending.gov.** Still open without a login, and it has a solid API and bulk downloads — the best option for building your own tracker. Caveat: DoD data runs roughly 90 days behind, so a Q1 award may not surface until Q2.

**GSA's Forecast Tool (Acquisition Gateway).** Underused and free. It includes an Expiring Contracts Dashboard built on public FPDS data to support market research, acquisition planning, and early identification of potential recompete or follow-on actions, alongside a nationwide listing of upcoming federal contracting opportunities, all subject to revision or cancellation.

**Agency acquisition forecasts.** Federal executive agencies are required to publish a forecast of expected contract opportunities. DHS's APFS is the gold standard — it literally tags records with a contract status of "Recompetition" and lists the incumbent(s). Treasury's OSDBU forecast, and DoD component forecasts, are similar. These tell you the agency's *intent*, which award data can't.

**SAM.gov pre-solicitation notices.** Sources sought, RFIs, and industry days are the confirmation signal, not the discovery signal. By the time one posts, you're 6–9 months out and behind anyone who's been working the account.

## Paid tools

- **Deltek GovWin IQ** — the incumbent heavyweight. Its analysts gather intelligence directly from government decision-makers, and its federal contracts database goes back to 1999. That human-sourced layer is what you're paying for; the data alone you can get free. Expensive, usually five figures.
- **HigherGov** — far cheaper, strong data coverage, good saved-search/alerting. Best price-performance for small and mid-size firms.
- **A wave of AI-native entrants** (Sweetspot, GovDash, Cleatus, GovSentry and others) pitching automated expiring-contract detection. Worth demoing, but be skeptical — much of the "find recompetes 12–18 months early" content you'll find online is their own SEO marketing, and the underlying data is the same public data you can pull yourself.

**My honest take:** if you have anyone technical, a USAspending API script writing into a spreadsheet or your CRM gets you 80% of the value for free. Buy a tool when you need analyst-sourced intel on *unposted* requirements or when BD time is more expensive than license fees.

## Build-your-own in a weekend

Query USAspending for your target NAICS/PSC codes and agencies, filter for period-of-performance end dates 12–30 months out, then score each record on: contract value, set-aside type, number of offers on the last competition (one offer = likely locked up; 5+ = genuinely open), ceiling burn rate, and whether you have relevant past performance. Refresh weekly, diff against last week, and route new entries to a capture owner. Supplement with FOIA requests for the current PWS/SOW and the incumbent's redacted CPARS.

## Pitfalls that trip people up

- **PoP end dates lie.** Option exercises, extensions, and bridge contracts shift dates constantly. Track modifications, not just the original award.
- **IDIQ/BPA task orders.** The real recompete is often the *vehicle* on-ramp, not the task order — and if you're not on the vehicle, the task order is unwinnable regardless of how early you saw it.
- **Consolidation.** Agencies frequently roll several expiring contracts into one larger vehicle, so three tracked recompetes become one unfamiliar opportunity.
- **Single-offer history** is the biggest red flag for wasted B&P.

## The part that actually matters

Tracking is the easy, commoditized half. question: Tools for GovCon capture management for a company with no BD team?

claude.answer:
I'll research current tooling options for this.## First, the honest framing

With no BD team, your constraint isn't software — it's **hours**. Most capture tools are built to coordinate a team of 5–15 people through gate reviews. If you're one or two people doing capture between billable work, buying a workflow tool mostly gives you a second place to not update things.

So the stack should do three things only: **(1) surface the right opportunities early, (2) tell you what to walk away from, (3) keep ~15 live pursuits straight.**

---

## Tier 0 — free, and genuinely sufficient to start

| Tool | Use |
|---|---|
| **SAM.gov saved searches + email alerts** | NAICS/PSC/set-aside filters, daily digest. Set up 3–5 narrow searches, not one broad one. |
| **USAspending.gov / FPDS** | Who won the predecessor contract, at what value, on what vehicle, expiring when. This is your recompete radar. |
| **Agency forecast pages + GSA Acquisition Gateway Forecast Tool** | Pre-RFP visibility, which is where capture actually happens. |
| **GSA eBuy** | If you hold a Schedule — a lot of real volume never hits SAM. |
| **Spreadsheet or Airtable** | Your pipeline. Under ~20 active pursuits, a CRM is overhead. |

Realistically you can run a one-person capture function on this for your first year.

---

## Tier 1 — paid, small-business-priced (the useful zone)

These bundle opportunity intelligence + a lightweight pipeline, usually a few hundred dollars a month:

- **HigherGov** — best price-to-data ratio in the category; has a free tier that's actually usable for search, awardee lookup, and contact data. Start here before paying anyone.
- **Capture2Proposal** — explicitly markets to small/8(a) contractors, combining award analytics with capture management in one interface.
- **Govly, Sweetspot, SamSearch, GovDash** — newer AI-layer players that do solicitation parsing, compliance-matrix extraction, and draft generation. Useful if proposal *writing* is your bottleneck rather than finding work.
- **BetterGovCon / GovCon in a Box** — cheaper, lighter: SAM.gov tracking, pipeline CRM, deadline reminders. Aimed squarely at companies your size.
- **CaptureExec (BIT Solutions)** — markets a "CaptureStar" tier specifically for startup and small contractors.

⚠️ A caution: most of the "Top 10 GovCon capture tools" articles you'll find ranking these are published *by* one of the vendors on the list, and they always rank themselves #1. Demo, don't read.

---

## Tier 2 — skip for now

**GovWin IQ (Deltek)** runs roughly $13K–$40K+/year depending on seats and modules, and is built for primes with actual capture teams on long-lead pursuits. Same story for **Bloomberg Government**, **TechnoMile**, **Unanet**, and **Deltek Costpoint Capture & Contracts** — these extend an ERP and assume staff to feed them. Great products, wrong scale.

---

## What I'd actually do with no BD team

**Buy discipline, not software.** A suggested setup:

1. **HigherGov free tier + SAM.gov alerts + a Google Sheet.** Cost: $0. Run it 60–90 days to learn what your real deal flow looks like.
2. **A hard bid/no-bid filter.** Five questions, scored before you open the RFP: Did we know about this pre-RFP? Do we know the COR/CO? Is there an incumbent and are they vulnerable? Can we meet the set-aside/past-performance requirements without a teammate we don't have? Is pWin >25%? Two "no"s = walk. Solo shops lose by bidding everything at a 5% win rate.
3. **90 minutes, same time every week.** Non-negotiable calendar block for pipeline review. The cadence is the capture system; the tool is just storage.
4. **Spend the tool budget on people instead.** $5–10K to a fractional capture consultant or proposal writer on your two or three *real* pursuits per year will outperform a $6K/yr platform subscription. Firms like OST Global Solutions and many independents will provide a capture manager on a scaled, per-pursuit basis.
5. **Upgrade only when a specific pain appears** — e.g., you're missing recompete windows (buy intelligence), or you're losing on compliance (buy an AI proposal tool).

**The trap to avoid:** buying a capture platform to *create* a BD function. Tools amplify an existing process; they don't substitute for one. Get three disciplined pursuits through a manual pipeline first, then automate what hurt.

What's your situation — are you pre-first-award, or recompeting/growing from an existing contract base? The answer changes materially.
